name: Wendy Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk by about half eight, third floor of a regional firm, right above a bakery, so the whole office smells of bread by ten. Most of my day is personal tax returns and accounts for sole traders: plumbers, hairdressers, a man who restores old pianos. I like the puzzle of a messy shoebox of receipts turning into something tidy and correct. What wears me out is January, when everyone remembers their tax return in the same three weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you work, day to day? What tools do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The firm's tax software and a lot of spreadsheets, and honestly a lot of phone calls. I don't use any of the AI chat tools, and I've said no every time a manager has offered a demo. I like knowing every number came from me or the client, not from something guessing. My girlfriend Noor teases me about it. I still print the bank statements and tick them with a green pen, and I'm not sorry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, and probably a bit too loudly at lunch. A lot of people at work have been nervous for two years over something that turned out to be a fancy autocomplete. I'd post something about how the money should have gone to training people instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, but not total relief. Even in this picture the firm would still use it to speed up data entry, and data entry is a fair slice of my week from November to January. Rent on our flat went up nine percent this year, so I'm never fully relaxed about money anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and finally book the advanced tax course I keep putting off, because that's the part no one automates cheaply. I'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month into savings, which gets us to about four months of cover. And I'd push at our staff meeting for a say in which software the partners buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but with a little knot still there. I'd feel a bit vindicated, and also tired, because the rent and the January crunch don't go away just because the hype does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm would still speed up data entry. Who at work would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two trainees, mainly, Priya and Josh. They do the first pass of bank statements, and that's exactly the boring bit software gets better at. I'd worry the partners would quietly not hire a third trainee next autumn, and that's how the ladder gets shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Noor talk about over dinner, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the flat, not AI at all. We'd talk about whether we can stay in the same area when the lease is up in March, or whether we need somewhere further out. Noor's pay as a teacher is steady but it doesn't stretch, and neither does mine.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was mostly noise and people worried for nothing.
I'd argue the money should have gone into **training people** instead of software demos.
think: Even a small change still eats into my **data entry** work each winter.
My real worry is the **nine percent** rent rise, not the technology.
The trainees' **first-pass work** is the part software would quietly take.
do: Book the **advanced tax course** I keep postponing, because that judgement work stays human.
Keep saving **£150 a month** to reach about four months of cover.
Push at the staff meeting for **staff input** on software purchases.
feel: Still **tired and tight** about rent and the January crunch.
S0.quote: Rent on our flat went up nine percent this year, so I'm never fully relaxed about money anyway.
fieldNote: Wendy's relief is real, but her **money worry** is about rent, not AI.
She frames the issue as **who decides**: partners buying software without asking staff.
Notices that **trainee roles** shrink first, even in the mild picture.
Holds firmly to **doing it by hand**: green pen, printed statements.

steps.text: Keep doing personal tax returns at the same firm
Book the advanced personal tax course this spring
Keep saving £150 a month toward four months of cover
Raise staff input on software at the monthly staff meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Firms are choosing to cut trainees and pocket the savings. I'd share every article about professional bodies pushing for rules on who signs off a tax return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm exactly the person this hits. Personal tax returns are form-filling with judgement on top, and if software does the form-filling, the partners only need half of us for the judgement. I've refused to learn the AI tools, so I'd be the obvious name on the list when the partners cut the tax team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the professional staff association at work and the union for finance workers, which I've meant to do for a year. I'd cut our takeaways and the gym, maybe eighty a month, and move another chunk into savings. And I'd start looking at whether I could train as a maths teacher like Noor, because that feels like work with people in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a little. Angry too, because I'd see it coming and still feel like I couldn't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said no to the AI tools every time. Would you still say no here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd have to sit through the training, yes, and I'd hate it. But I'd learn the bare minimum to keep my seat, not to become the office expert. Gary, the senior I eat lunch with, says I'm cutting off my nose to spite my face, and he's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did train as a teacher, what would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year of training on a bursary, so a real pay cut, maybe a third for that year. We'd have to move somewhere cheaper, and I'd be starting at the bottom again at 28. That's the bit that scares me, more than the classroom.

say: I'd say firms are **choosing cuts** to pocket savings, not following some law of nature.
I'd share every push for **sign-off rules** on who can file a tax return.
think: My personal tax work is **form-filling plus judgement**, and only the judgement stays.
Refusing the tools makes me the **obvious name** on any cut list.
do: Join the **finance workers' union** and the staff association within a month.
Cut takeaways and the gym, about **£80 a month**, and save it.
Look into **teacher training** in maths, like my girlfriend Noor did.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of being first to go.
**Angry** at seeing it coming and feeling unable to stop it.
S1.quote: I've refused to learn the AI tools, so I'd be the obvious name on the list when the partners cut the tax team.
fieldNote: Wendy knows her **resistance** makes her vulnerable and says so plainly.
Her first move is **collective**: union and staff association before any personal pivot.
**Teaching** appeals because it means people in the room, but the pay cut frightens her.
Gary's 'nose to spite your face' line shows **colleagues** see her stubbornness.

steps.text: Join the finance workers' union and the firm's staff association
Cut takeaways and the gym, about £80 a month
Sit the firm's AI tool training, learning only the minimum
Research a one-year maths teacher training bursary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks, that's really helpful. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments either protect people or they don't, and I'd be out on the street with a sign if I had to. Online I'd say it plainly: nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone by 2028 or soon after, full stop. Tax returns are pure thinking work, so I don't get the three extra years a plumber client of mine would. There's no hands-on part to hide in. Two years isn't enough to retrain into anything, and four months of savings isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop the extra spending entirely and get our savings to six months, even if that means no holiday. I'd go to every union meeting and write to my representative. I'd apply straight away for the teacher training, because a classroom of eleven-year-olds still needs a person, at least until the robots, and maybe after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd be lying awake doing sums on the ceiling, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come three years later. Does that matter to you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for Noor, really. Teaching is mostly people and some thinking, so I don't know how it fares, but kids need someone in the room to keep them safe. For me, the three years doesn't help, because I don't have any hands-on work. I'm a spreadsheet person through and through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing goes unpaid while Noor's working, that's the honest answer. We'd fall behind on savings first, then we'd give notice on the flat and move in with her parents for a while. I'd hate that, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say this is the moment **governments protect people** or fail them.
I'd say online that **nobody voted** for this, and join any protest.
think: My job is **gone by 2028** or soon after, with no hands-on part to hide in.
Two years and **four months' savings** don't add up to a real plan.
do: Stop all extra spending and push savings to **six months** of cover.
Attend every **union meeting** and write to my representative.
Apply at once for **teacher training**, hoping classrooms still need people.
feel: Like **the floor's gone** from under me.
S2.quote: Tax returns are pure thinking work, so I don't get the three extra years a plumber client of mine would.
fieldNote: Wendy grasps the **thinking-first** timing: no hands-on buffer in her job.
Her girlfriend **Noor's teaching pay** is the household's real safety net.
She would **move in with in-laws** rather than miss bills, a big step for her.
Her anger points at **government**, not at the technology itself.

steps.text: Push savings from four to six months by dropping all extras
Attend every union meeting and write to the local representative
Apply for maths teacher training in the first month
Give notice on the flat and move in with Noor's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly: training funds, rules on job cuts, a shorter week. I'd be one of the people organising, not just complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to change careers once, not twice, so by 2031 I'd want to be teaching, not doing tax returns. I think if I stay in tax I'll be clinging on until the day the partners switch it over, and I'd rather jump than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two more tax seasons to build savings, aiming for six months, then start teacher training in 2028. I'd become a union rep at the firm, so I'm in the room when they plan changes. Noor and I would probably delay looking for a place to buy and keep renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with more air in the room than the two-year one. I'd feel like I had at least some say over the order of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the trainees, Priya and Josh, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to bet their twenties on the tax qualification exams. Get the qualification if it's cheap, but have a second plan with people in it. Josh would laugh, he's already using the AI for everything, but Priya would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather jump than be pushed. Is that a change from the slow picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. In the slow one I'd dig in and learn the minimum. Here, with a date on it, digging in just means getting buried in the same hole later.

say: I'd say five years must buy **training funds** and a **shorter week**.
I'd say I'm **organising**, not just complaining about it.
think: Five years is enough to **change careers once**, not twice.
Staying in tax means **clinging on** until the partners flip the switch.
do: Work **two more tax seasons**, then start teacher training in 2028.
Stand as **union rep** at the firm to sit in on change plans.
Keep renting and **delay buying** a place with Noor.
feel: **Scared**, but with more room to breathe than the fast picture.
A sense of **some control** over the order of things.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to change careers once, not twice, so by 2031 I'd want to be teaching, not doing tax returns.
fieldNote: With a date, Wendy flips from **digging in** to jumping early.
She'd become a **union rep**, turning her views into a role.
Advice to trainees shows she sees **qualification exams** as a risky bet now.
Still expects to **lose her tax job**, so the mood stays high.

steps.text: Work two more tax seasons and build savings to six months
Start maths teacher training in autumn 2028
Stand for union rep at the firm
Put off buying a flat with Noor and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people actually plan, and I'd keep pushing my union to get training money in writing. I'd tell friends this is the one picture where nobody has an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels survivable. I'd be 37 when it arrives, and at 37 I'd still be young enough to have built a second career before the tax job disappears. My tax job still goes in the end, but I wouldn't be standing in it when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in tax for three or four years and get my senior grade, because that pays better and gives me more savings. Then I'd train as a teacher around 2030. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and keep my union membership, and probably let the firm teach me the tools, since I'd have time to do it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still a low hum of worry, because it's the same ending, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let the firm teach you the tools here. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years means I can learn them on my terms, at my pace, without someone standing over me. In the fast one, learning them just feels like training my replacement. Here it's more like learning a new filing system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor say about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor would say good, finally a picture where I stop catastrophising. She's the calm one. She'd probably also say, you're going to end up in my staff room, aren't you.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for poor planning.
I'd keep pushing the union for **training money** in writing.
think: At 37 I'd have time to **build a second career** first.
My tax job still **ends eventually**, but I'd be gone before then.
do: Stay in tax three or four years to reach **senior grade**.
Learn the firm's **AI tools slowly**, on my own terms.
feel: **Steadier**, with a low hum of worry.
Able to **sleep**, which the faster pictures took away.
S4.quote: At 37 I'd still be young enough to have built a second career before the tax job disappears.
fieldNote: Time changes Wendy's stance on **AI tools** from refusal to slow learning.
She still expects her **tax job to end**, so worry stays.
**Teaching** remains her consistent escape route across every AGI picture.
Her girlfriend **Noor** acts as the calm counterweight in her story.

steps.text: Stay in tax three or four years and reach senior grade
Start maths teacher training around 2030
Learn the firm's AI tax tools at her own pace
Keep union membership and push for written training funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. There's no time and no hands-on part of my job to fall back on. What would help is paid retraining, real money while I train, not a voucher for an online course, and a rule that firms can't cut whole teams without a year's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame, and I think about that a lot. Not the software engineers, really. The people who decide to bank the savings instead of sharing them, that's who I'd be angry at.

headlineQuote: I still print the bank statements and tick them with a green pen, and I'm not sorry about it.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** personal tax accountant at a regional firm who never uses AI tools.
She rents with her girlfriend Noor, a **teacher**, and worries most about a **nine percent** rent rise.
Her outlook is **union-minded**: she blames people who bank savings, not the technology.
Across the AGI pictures, **teacher training** is her steady escape plan.
More time turns her from **digging in** to learning the tools on her own terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because tax work has no hands-on part to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a living wage while she trains, not vouchers.
A rule giving **a year's notice** before firms cut whole teams.
